title: Bloom Security lands $20 million seed as AI rewrites what runs on the enterprise endpoint

content_html:
TL;DR

Bloom Security has raised $20M in seed funding led by Glilot Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures to secure the AI-era endpoint. The company argues that EDR was built for malware, not for the AI agents, MCP servers, browser extensions, and code packages now running on every employee device. Its platform provides contextual visibility across all endpoint software and enforces risk-based policies without blanket lockdowns. Already deployed at dozens of large US and European enterprises.

Work does not look like it did three years ago. Employees now assemble their own toolkits daily: AI agents that act on their behalf, browser extensions that reshape how they read and write, code packages pulled from public registries, MCP servers connecting one tool to another. AI tools are no longer optional. They are how modern work gets done. The device on every desk has quietly become an ecosystem, and almost none of the security stack guarding it was built with that in mind.

Into this gap steps Bloom Security, which launched from stealth today with a $20 million seed round, first reported by Axios, led by Glilot Capital Partners and Ten Eleven Ventures (1011vc), with participation from Okta Ventures and Runtime Ventures, plus angel backing from founders of Dig Security, Demisto, Snyk, and Talon.

The Shape of the Shift

The Tel Aviv-based company describes the enterprise endpoint as fundamentally shifted. What were once managed, predictable devices are now assemblages of agentic software, MCP servers, browser extensions, and code packages. Browsers, IDEs, and AI agents ship with their own app stores and marketplaces, which means the software layer on employee devices grows faster than any security team can track. Existing security infrastructure was never built to see it.

“In the AI era, the employee device is no longer just a managed endpoint,” said Itay Keren, Co-Founder and CEO of Bloom Security. “Every endpoint is now running software no one reviewed, connecting to services no one provisioned.”

The industry’s incumbent answer, endpoint detection and response, was engineered for a different threat model. EDR hunts malware: binaries, executables, malicious processes. But on the modern endpoint, malware is only part of the problem. The risks that keep security leaders awake are now often legitimate tools in the wrong state. A misconfigured AI agent. A plugin with excessive data permissions. A screen recorder on an executive’s laptop. A code library pulling from an untrusted source. Each is an everyday tool capable of creating a dangerous attack path. Risk starts with what is already running, and most security teams lack a way to control it.

The company’s answer is a full-scope endpoint security architecture that integrates deep contextual visibility, proactive enforcement, granular remediation, and proactive prevention in one platform. The intent is not to lock devices down. It is to bring order to the inherent complexity of the modern endpoint so that productivity tools can be used to their full potential, free from unnecessary risk.

In practice, the platform gives security teams a holistic view of every piece of software running across every endpoint, from tools to extensions to code, along with how each interacts with data and systems. It analyzes supply chain risk. It examines configurations and permissions to determine actual exposure.

The product’s defining idea is that risk is situational. “The same tool can be completely acceptable on one endpoint and high-risk on another,” said Ofir Balassiano, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Bloom Security. “Risk depends on context: the user’s role, their access to sensitive data, the other tools operating on that endpoint, their configurations, and how everything interacts. Bloom Security was designed to evaluate that context in real time.”

Visibility feeds action. Teams can block risky installs before they reach employee endpoints, enforce secure configurations directly, and remediate risks without manual approval workflows or disruption to how employees work.

“As AI adoption accelerated, it became clear that existing endpoint controls were not designed for this new reality,” Keren added. “Security teams need a way to understand, govern, and control modern tools without disrupting how employees work.”

A Team That Has Done This Before

Bloom Security’s founders arrive with acquisition credentials. CEO Itay Keren held engineering and sales engineering leadership roles at Palo Alto Networks, Dig Security (acquired by Palo Alto Networks), and Demisto (also acquired by Palo Alto Networks). He served as a Naval Officer before entering cybersecurity, leading teams in high-pressure environments.

Chief Product Officer Ofir Balassiano led the Cortex Cloud Posture Security research group at Palo Alto Networks, working on AI, identity, and data security. Earlier, he led the research group at Dig Security and served as a Senior Security Researcher at XM Cyber. His career began in the IDF’s Mamram Unit.

Chief Technology Officer Itay Frishman built core AISPM and DSPM solutions at Palo Alto Networks and Dig Security, after cybersecurity R&D leadership in the IDF’s Unit 81.

“While this is technically our first company as founders, our team has built and integrated category-defining products before,” Frishman said. “We understand how enterprise security environments operate, and we built Bloom Security specifically for the reality of how endpoints are used today.”

The company employs 30 people today, many of whom worked together at Dig Security.

Early Traction, Bigger Ambitions

Despite only now leaving stealth, Bloom Security is already deployed at dozens of large enterprises across the United States and Europe. Those customers are gaining total visibility into their endpoints and swapping rigid, blanket policies for precise, contextual remediation. The company’s focus is large enterprises navigating AI adoption at scale.

That early footprint drew notice from its lead investor. “AI has changed the enterprise endpoint in ways the security industry is still catching up to. Agents, MCP servers, browser extensions, and code packages now run on every employee’s machine, entirely outside the reach of traditional controls,” said Kobi Samboursky, Founder and Managing Partner at Glilot Capital. “Bloom identified this gap before the market did, and the business traction we’ve seen in their first months is unprecedented for a company at this stage. A team this experienced with a problem this urgent and momentum this strong is what category-defining companies look like from day one.”

The broader story here is about a lag. Workplaces adopted AI tools at consumer speed while security controls moved at enterprise speed. That gap between how people work and how their devices are protected is exactly where Bloom Security has planted its flag. The next few years will show whether the AI-native endpoint becomes a recognized security category. Today’s launch makes clear that serious money believes it will.

content_html_zh:
TL;DR

Bloom Security 已筹集 2000 万美元种子资金，由 Glilot Capital 和 Ten Eleven Ventures 牵头，以确保 AI 时代端点的安全。 该公司辩称，EDR 是为恶意软件而构建的，而不是为现在每个员工设备上运行的 AI 代理、MCP 服务器、浏览器扩展和代码包而构建的。 其平台提供跨所有端点软件的上下文可见性，并执行基于风险的策略，而无需全面锁定。 已部署于数十家欧美大型企业。

工作看起来已经不像三年前了。 员工现在每天组装自己的工具包：代表他们行事的人工智能代理、重塑他们读写方式的浏览器扩展、从公共注册表中提取的代码包、将一种工具连接到另一种工具的 MCP 服务器。 人工智能工具不再是可选的。 它们是现代工作的完成方式。 每张桌子上的设备已经悄然成为一个生态系统，几乎没有一个保护它的安全堆栈是考虑到这一点而构建的。

Bloom Security 填补了这一空白，该公司今天秘密推出了 2000 万美元种子轮融资，最先由 Axios 报道，由 Glilot Capital Partners 和 Ten Eleven Ventures (1011vc) 牵头，Okta Ventures 和 Runtime Ventures 参与，还有 Dig Security、Demisto、Snyk 和 Talon 创始人的天使投资。

转变的形式

这家总部位于特拉维夫的公司将企业端点描述为发生了根本性转变。 曾经受管理的、可预测的设备现在是代理软件、MCP 服务器、浏览器扩展和代码包的集合。 浏览器、IDE 和 AI 代理附带自己的应用程序商店和市场，这意味着员工设备上的软件层的增长速度比任何安全团队都可以跟踪。 现有的安全基础设施从来都不是为了看到这一点而构建的。

Bloom Security 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Itay Keren 表示：“在人工智能时代，员工设备不再只是一个托管端点。” “现在每个端点都运行着无人审查的软件，连接着无人提供的服务。”

业界现有的解决方案——端点检测和响应——是针对不同的威胁模型而设计的。 EDR 搜寻恶意软件：二进制文件、可执行文件、恶意进程。 但在现代端点上，恶意软件只是问题的一部分。 现在，让安全领导者保持清醒的风险往往是处于错误状态的合法工具。 AI 代理配置错误。 具有过多数据权限的插件。 高管笔记本电脑上的屏幕录像机。 从不受信任的来源提取的代码库。 每一个都是能够创建危险攻击路径的日常工具。 风险始于已经运行的内容，大多数安全团队缺乏控制它的方法。

该公司的答案是一种全方位的端点安全架构，将深度上下文可见性、主动执行、精细修复和主动预防集成在一个平台中。 目的不是锁定设备。 它旨在使现代端点固有的复杂性变得有序，以便生产力工具可以充分发挥其潜力，而无需承担不必要的风险。

在实践中，该平台为安全团队提供了跨每个端点运行的每个软件的整体视图，从工具到扩展再到代码，以及每个软件如何与数据和系统交互。 它分析供应链风险。 它检查配置和权限以确定实际暴露情况。

该产品的定义理念是风险是视情况而定的。 Bloom Security 联合创始人兼首席产品官 Ofir Balassiano 表示：“同一个工具在一个端点上完全可以接受，但在另一个端点上却存在高风险。” “风险取决于上下文：用户的角色、他们对敏感数据的访问、在该端点上运行的其他工具、他们的配置以及一切交互的方式。 Bloom Security 旨在实时评估该环境。”

可见性促进行动。 团队可以在有风险的安装到达员工端点之前阻止它们，直接实施安全配置，并修复风险，而无需手动审批工作流程或中断员工的工作方式。

“随着人工智能采用的加速，很明显现有的端点控制并不是针对这一新现实而设计的，”Keren 补充道。 “安全团队需要一种方法来理解、管理和控制现代工具，同时又不影响员工的工作方式。”

以前做过这样的团队

Bloom Security 的创始人带着收购凭证前来。 首席执行官 Itay Keren 曾在 Palo Alto Networks、Dig Security（被 Palo Alto Networks 收购）和 Demisto（也被 Palo Alto Networks 收购）担任工程和销售工程领导职务。 在进入网络安全领域之前，他曾担任海军军官，在高压环境下领导团队。

首席产品官 Ofir Balassiano 领导 Palo Alto Networks 的 Cortex Cloud Posture Security 研究小组，致力于人工智能、身份和数据安全。 此前，他曾领导 Dig Security 的研究小组，并担任 XM Cyber​​ 的高级安全研究员。 他的职业生涯始于以色列国防军的马姆拉姆部队。

首席技术官 Itay Frishman 在 IDF Unit 81 的网络安全研发领导地位之后，在 Palo Alto Networks 和 Dig Security 构建了核心 AISPM 和 DSPM 解决方案。

“虽然从技术上讲，这是我们作为创始人创办的第一家公司，但我们的团队之前已经构建并集成了类别定义产品，”Frishman 说。 “我们了解企业安全环境的运作方式，并且我们专门针对当今端点使用的现实情况构建了 Bloom Security。”

该公司目前拥有 30 名员工，其中许多人在 Dig Security 工作。

早期牵引力，更大的野心

尽管 Bloom Security 现在才处于隐秘状态，但它已经部署在美国和欧洲的数十家大型企业中。 这些客户正在获得对其端点的全面可见性，并将严格的一揽子策略转变为精确的上下文修复。 该公司的重点是大型企业大规模采用人工智能。

早期的足迹引起了其主要投资者的注意。 “人工智能以安全行业仍在追赶的方式改变了企业端点。 代理、MCP 服务器、浏览器扩展和代码包现在运行在每个员工的机器上，完全超出了传统控制的范围。”Glilot Capital 创始人兼管理合伙人 Kobi Samboursky 说道。 “布鲁姆在市场出现之前就发现了这一差距，我们在头几个月看到的业务牵引力对于现阶段的公司来说是前所未有的。 一支经历过如此紧迫问题、动力如此强劲的团队从第一天起就是定义类别的公司的样子。”

这里更广泛的故事是关于滞后的。 工作场所以消费者的速度采用人工智能工具，而安全控制以企业的速度发展。 人们的工作方式和设备的保护方式之间的差距正是 Bloom Security 所立下的旗帜。 未来几年将展示人工智能原生端点是否成为公认的安全类别。 今天的发布清楚地表明，严肃的资金相信它会实现。
